profiles.name: David Bobbitt
profiles.description: David Bobbitt was a Marine reservist from Staten Island who refused Gulf War deployment. Contemporary reporting identified him among the military resisters prosecuted for refusing service and reported a 14-month prison sentence.
profiles.finding: CSPG90697 Hands Off poster individually names Bobbitt and Staten Island identity. Downloaded public scan334x450; individual faces roughly30-40px wide, unusably small. Higher-resolution archive lead remains.
profiles.rights: No image selected; see shared lead and source credits.

profiles.name: Frederick LeVelle McKinney
profiles.description: Frederick LeVelle McKinney was a 25-year-old Marine lance corporal from Forestville, Maryland, who applied for conscientious-objector status and refused Gulf War service. After a short unauthorized absence, he turned himself in at Camp Lejeune and faced military charges alongside other reservists. Contemporary reporting on April 16, 1991 explicitly described McKinney and the other nine Marines awaiting hearings as not confined. The final disposition of his charges has not been located.
profiles.query: "Frederick LeVelle McKinney" Gulf War resister photo
profiles.finding: Washington Post1991 and CSPG caption Lavelle McKinney support identity; poster details differ from current case chronology, no non-photo fields changed. Public scan too small for portrait.
profiles.rights: No image selected; see shared lead and source credits.

profiles.name: Paul E. Cook
profiles.description: Paul E. Cook was a U.S. Marine whose opposition to war developed after service in Panama. After his conscientious-objector application was rejected, he deployed to the Gulf but refused to carry a weapon, offering to perform medical-evacuation radio work instead. He was court-martialed and imprisoned at Camp Lejeune.
profiles.query: "Paul E. Cook" Gulf War resister photo
profiles.finding: CSPG poster identifies Paul Cook active-duty Marine; public face crop too small. WWII Cook1905-2003 and elderly obituary namesakes rejected.
profiles.rights: No image selected; see shared lead and source credits.

profiles.name: Marquis Leacock
profiles.description: Marquis Leacock was a U.S. Marine who sought conscientious-objector status after a training accident deepened his opposition to killing. He was convicted of desertion, received a bad-conduct discharge, and served six months of confinement. He later returned to college.
profiles.finding: Swarthmore Rosa Packard papers include correspondence; CSPG identifies Leacock, but public face crop too small.
profiles.rights: No image selected; see shared lead and source credits.

profiles.name: David Wiggins
profiles.description: David Wiggins was a U.S. Army captain and physician who sought conscientious-objector status during the Gulf War. He protested his deployment, including by removing his uniform in Riyadh. His court-martial resulted in dismissal from the Army and a $25,000 fine, rather than a prison sentence.
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist and War Resisters2021 identify Army physician; USAF staff sergeant and British philosopher rejected. No verified portrait.

profiles.name: Jody Anderson
profiles.description: Jody Anderson was a U.S. Marine prosecuted after intervening when fellow resister Danny Gillis was being forcibly taken for deployment. Anderson himself deployed to the Gulf. He later received a two-year sentence; a retrospective reports that he served two years.
profiles.finding: Fifth Estate1992 and Solidarity match Jody Anderson; contemporary Florida mugshot not independently matched, rejected.

profiles.name: James Moss
profiles.description: James Moss was a U.S. Navy sailor aboard USS Ranger accused, with a fellow sailor, of encouraging resistance to Gulf War service. The allegations included mutiny and sabotage-related activity. A later historical account reports that the charges were dropped in 1992. The accusations are not treated as established conduct.
profiles.finding: Bridgeman REU12024477 is captioned two-sailor image dated1991-04-01 by Romeo Ranoco/Reuters. Licensed source; individual position and usable authorized file pending. Air Force loadmaster and Canadian war casualty rejected.

profiles.name: Robert Pete
profiles.description: Robert Pete was a Louisiana National Guardsman prosecuted after soldiers protested conditions during Gulf War mobilization at Fort Hood. He received a six-year sentence in 1991. The Army Court of Military Review subsequently set aside his conviction, finding the evidence insufficient to establish the charged strike-related offenses.
profiles.finding: UPI1991 and Virginia Tech archive match Louisiana guardsman; Library of Congress blues musician Robert Pete Williams and WWII pilot rejected.
profiles.rights: No image selected; see shared lead and source credits.

profiles.name: Derrick Guidry
profiles.description: Derrick Guidry was a Louisiana National Guardsman prosecuted after a soldiers' protest at Fort Hood during Gulf War mobilization. He was acquitted of the strike-related charges but convicted of disrespect toward a superior officer. His punishment was a $500 fine and reduction in rank, with no prison sentence.
profiles.finding: Texas Tech Snyder October1991 and Virginia Tech news archives match case; IMDb namesake not independently matched. No portrait verified.
profiles.rights: No image selected; see shared lead and source credits.

profiles.name: Tim Brassil
profiles.description: Tim Brassil was a British Army reservist and former Army nurse who refused a Gulf War call-up in January 1991. He went into hiding and linked his opposition to the war with concern over health-service funding. This United Kingdom military-resistance case has no verified prison sentence in the reviewed account.
profiles.finding: Libcom Gulf War resistance pamphlet confirms former Army nurse; no verified portrait found.
profiles.rights: No image selected; see shared lead and source credits.
